## 3. The arithmetic layer: two types and a deterministic law

### 3.1 The defining cubic

**Definition 3.1.** $f(x) = x^3 + x^2 - 2x - 1$, and $K = \mathbb{Q}[x]/(f)$.

**Proposition 3.2 (Cyclotomic substitution).** For any field $L$ and any nonzero $y \in L$,
$$y^3\, f\!\left(y + y^{-1}\right) = 1 + y + y^2 + y^3 + y^4 + y^5 + y^6.$$

*Proof.* Expand $(y+y^{-1})^3 + (y+y^{-1})^2 - 2(y+y^{-1}) - 1$ and multiply by $y^3$. $\square$

**Corollary 3.3.** If $y^7 = 1$ and $y \neq 1$, then $y + y^{-1}$ is a root of $f$. In particular $\zeta_7 + \zeta_7^{-1} = 2\cos(2\pi/7)$ is a root, and $f$ is its minimal polynomial over $\mathbb{Q}$; $f$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ (indeed already modulo $2$), so $K$ is a cubic field, and $K = \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_7+\zeta_7^{-1})$ is the real subfield of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_7)$, cyclic of degree $3$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.

### 3.2 Splitting is all-or-nothing

**Definition 3.4 (Frobenius twist).** On roots of $f$, set $\tau(x) = x^2 - 2$. This is the polynomial shadow of $\zeta + \zeta^{-1} \mapsto \zeta^2 + \zeta^{-2}$.

**Lemma 3.5.** Over any commutative ring, if $f(x) = 0$ then $f(x^2-2) = 0$. If moreover $7$ is invertible (more precisely, if $7 \neq 0$ in an integral domain containing $x$), then $x^2 - 2 \neq x$ and $(x^2-2)^2 - 2 \neq x$.

*Proof sketch.* The first assertion is a polynomial identity: $f(x^2-2)$ lies in the ideal generated by $f(x)$, verified by expansion. For the second, $x^2 - 2 = x$ would force $x$ to satisfy $x^2 - x - 2 = 0$ simultaneously with $f(x) = 0$; eliminating gives $7 = 0$. The third is the analogous elimination with $\tau^2$. $\square$

**Theorem 3.6 (All-or-nothing splitting).** Let $D$ be an integral domain with $7 \neq 0$. If $f$ has one root $x \in D$, then $f$ has three distinct roots $x$, $\tau(x)$, $\tau^2(x)$ in $D$ and splits completely:
$$f(X) = (X - x)(X - \tau(x))(X - \tau^2(x)).$$

*Proof.* By Lemma 3.5 the three elements are roots and pairwise distinct (distinctness of $\tau(x)$ and $\tau^2(x)$ follows by applying the argument to $\tau(x)$). A monic cubic with three distinct roots in a domain factors as stated. $\square$

Consequently, for a prime $p \neq 7$, the factorisation type of $f$ modulo $p$ is either "three linear factors" or "irreducible": the residue degrees are all $1$ or all $3$. There is no $1+2$ pattern. (This is of course consistent with $\mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q}) \cong \mathbb{Z}/3$ having no elements of order $2$, but the argument above is elementary and self-contained.)

### 3.3 The splitting criterion

**Theorem 3.7 (Cyclic cubic splitting criterion).** Let $p \neq 7$ be prime. Then
$$\exists\, x \in \mathbb{F}_p:\ f(x) = 0 \iff p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 7 .$$
Equivalently, $p$ splits completely in $K$ (residue degree $1$) iff $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 7$, and is inert (residue degree $3$) otherwise.

*Proof sketch.* ($\Leftarrow$, case $p \equiv 1$.) Then $\mathbb{F}_p^\times$ is cyclic of order $p - 1$ divisible by $7$, so it contains an element $y$ of order $7$; by Corollary 3.3, $x = y + y^{-1}$ is a root.

($\Leftarrow$, case $p \equiv -1$.) Now $\mathbb{F}_p$ has no element of order $7$, but $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$ does, because $7 \mid p^2 - 1$. Take $y \in \mathbb{F}_{p^2}$ of order $7$ and set $x = y + y^{-1}$. The Frobenius $z \mapsto z^p$ sends $y \mapsto y^p = y^{-1}$ (as $p \equiv -1 \bmod 7$), hence fixes $x$; so $x \in \mathbb{F}_p$ and is a root of $f$.

($\Rightarrow$.) Suppose $f(x) = 0$ with $x \in \mathbb{F}_p$. Let $M = \begin{pmatrix} x & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, the companion matrix of $Y^2 - xY + 1$: $\det M = 1$, $\operatorname{tr} M = x$, and $M^2 = xM - I$. Iterating yields $M^{n+1} = A_{n+1}(x) M - A_n(x) I$ with the Chebyshev-type recursion $A_0 = 0$, $A_1 = 1$, $A_{n+2} = t A_{n+1} - A_n$. One computes $A_7(t) = t^6 - 5t^4 + 6t^2 - 1$ and $A_6(t) = t^5 - 4t^3 + 3t$, and checks the polynomial identities
$$A_7(t) = -f(t)\,f(-t), \qquad A_6(t) + 1 = f(t)\cdot\left(t^2 - t - 1\right),$$
so that $f(x) = 0$ forces $A_7(x) = 0$ and $A_6(x) = -1$, i.e. $M^7 = I$ while $M \neq I$: $M$ has order exactly $7$ in $SL_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$. A non-scalar element of $SL_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$ of order $m$ coprime to $p$ satisfies $m \mid p^2 - 1$ (its eigenvalues are primitive $m$-th roots of unity in $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}^\times$, a cyclic group of order $p^2-1$). Hence $7 \mid (p-1)(p+1)$, i.e. $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 7$. $\square$

**Definition 3.8 (Type map).** For a nonzero residue $r \in \mathbb{Z}/7$ define the residue degree
$$d(r) = \begin{cases} 1 & r \in \{1, 6\},\\ 3 & \text{otherwise},\end{cases}$$
and the Boolean type $T(r) = [\,d(r) = 1\,] = [\,r \in \{\pm 1\}\,]$.

**Corollary 3.9 (Only two types; determinism).** $d(r) \in \{1, 3\}$ for all $r$, and if $p \equiv q \pmod 7$ then $d(p) = d(q)$. The type of an unramified prime is a *function* of its residue class. This is the fact that drives everything in Sections 5–7.

### 3.4 The conductor-free mechanism

The proof of the hard direction never used $7$. Define, for a commutative ring $R$ and $t \in R$, the sequence $A_n(t)$ as above, and let $C(t) = \begin{pmatrix} t & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$.

**Theorem 3.10 (Trace-order criterion).** Let $p$ and $m$ be primes with $m$ odd and $m \neq p$. The following are equivalent:
1. there is $t \in \mathbb{F}_p$ with $A_m(t) = 0$ and $A_{m-1}(t) = -1$;
2. $C(t)$ has order exactly $m$ in $SL_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$ for some $t$;
3. $m \mid p^2 - 1$, i.e. $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod m$.

*Proof sketch.* $(1) \Leftrightarrow (2)$ from $C(t)^{m} = A_m(t)C(t) - A_{m-1}(t)I$ together with $C(t) \neq I$ and $C(t)$ non-scalar. $(2) \Rightarrow (3)$: eigenvalues of an order-$m$ non-scalar element lie in $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}^\times$, cyclic of order $p^2-1$. $(3) \Rightarrow (2)$: take $y \in \mathbb{F}_{p^2}$ of order $m$ with $y + y^{-1} \in \mathbb{F}_p$ (Frobenius-stable since $y^p \in \{y, y^{-1}\}$), and use $t = y + y^{-1}$. $\square$

**Corollary 3.11 (Specialisations).** For $p \neq 5$: $x^2 + x - 1$ has a root mod $p$ iff $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 5$ (golden-ratio / Fibonacci criterion). For $p \neq 7$: $x^3 + x^2 - 2x - 1$ has a root mod $p$ iff $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 7$ (a second, independent proof of Theorem 3.7). For $p \neq 11$: $x^5 + x^4 - 4x^3 - 3x^2 + 3x + 1$, the minimal polynomial of $\zeta_{11}+\zeta_{11}^{-1}$, has a root mod $p$ iff $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{11}$.

In each case the bridge from Theorem 3.10 to the corollary is a pair of explicit polynomial identities over $\mathbb{Z}[t]$: a factorisation of $A_m(t)$ having the minimal polynomial $\Psi_m$ of $\zeta_m + \zeta_m^{-1}$ as one factor, and an identity expressing $A_{m-1}(t) + 1$ as $\Psi_m(t)$ times a cofactor coprime to $\Psi_m$ modulo every $p \nmid m$. Both were verified by direct expansion for $m = 5, 7, 11$; the uniform-in-$m$ statement is Conjecture 9.1 below.

## 4. The information-theoretic layer

The following two statements are completely general — they hold for arbitrary finite joint laws — and they are what turns the arithmetic determinism of Corollary 3.9 into a sharp information identity.

**Theorem 4.1 (Marginalisation decreases entropy).** Let $A$, $B$ be finite sets and $w : A\times B \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ with $\sum w \le 1$. Then
$$H(w_A) \le H(w) \quad\text{and}\quad H(w_B) \le H(w).$$

*Proof.* Split the joint sum along fibres: $H(w) = \sum_{a\in A} \sum_{b \in B}\eta(w(a,b))$, and apply Lemma 2.1 in each fibre to get $\sum_b \eta(w(a,b)) \ge \eta(\sum_b w(a,b)) = \eta(w_A(a))$. Sum over $a$. The other statement is symmetric. $\square$

**Theorem 4.2 (Data-processing ceiling).** With $w$ as above,
$$I(w) \le H(w_A) \qquad\text{and}\qquad I(w) \le H(w_B).$$

*Proof.* $I(w) = H(w_A) + H(w_B) - H(w) \le H(w_A) + H(w_B) - H(w_B) = H(w_A)$ by Theorem 4.1 applied to the $B$-marginal; symmetrically for the other. $\square$

**Theorem 4.3 (Determinism saturates the ceiling).** Let $g : A \to B$ be any map and $v : A \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ any weight. Define the joint law supported on the graph of $g$:
$$w(a,b) = \begin{cases} v(a) & b = g(a),\\ 0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
Then
$$I(w) = H(w_B) = H\!\left(b \mapsto \sum_{a : g(a) = b} v(a)\right).$$

*Proof.* The $A$-marginal is $w_A = v$, since exactly one $b$ contributes to each row. The joint entropy is $H(w) = \sum_a \sum_b \eta(w(a,b)) = \sum_a \eta(v(a)) = H(v)$, because all off-graph terms vanish and $\eta(0) = 0$. Hence
$$I(w) = H(v) + H(w_B) - H(v) = H(w_B). \qquad\square$$

Theorems 4.2 and 4.3 together say: *the mutual information of a channel is at most the entropy of its output, with equality whenever the output is a deterministic function of the input.* The converse also holds for strictly positive input weights (equality forces each row to be concentrated at a single output), so "fully pinned" and "deterministic" are the same condition.

---

## 5. The single-prime channel: full pinning

### 5.1 The joint law

**Definition 5.1.** Let $A = \mathbb{Z}/7$, $B = \{\text{split}, \text{inert}\}$ identified with $\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$, and
$$w_{\mathrm{RT}}(n, b) = \begin{cases} 1/6 & n \neq 0 \text{ and } b = T(n),\\ 0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
This is the joint law of $(p \bmod 7, T(p))$ in the uniform prime model. It is a probability law: exactly six of the fourteen cells carry $1/6$.

**Lemma 5.2 (Marginals).** $w_A(n) = 1/6$ for $n \neq 0$ and $0$ for $n = 0$; $w_B(\text{split}) = 1/3$, $w_B(\text{inert}) = 2/3$.

*Proof.* Immediate: two of six invertible classes ($1$ and $6$) are of split type. $\square$

### 5.2 Exact entropies

**Theorem 5.3 (Type entropy).** $\displaystyle H(T) = \log_2 3 - \tfrac23 = 0.9182958\ldots$ bits.

*Proof.* $H(T) = \eta(1/3) + \eta(2/3) = \tfrac13\log_2 3 + \tfrac23\log_2\tfrac32 = \tfrac13\log_2 3 + \tfrac23(\log_2 3 - 1) = \log_2 3 - \tfrac23$. $\square$

**Theorem 5.4 (Residue and joint entropy).** $H(R) = \log_2 6 = 1 + \log_2 3$, and $H(R,T) = \log_2 6 = 1 + \log_2 3$.

*Proof.* Both distributions are uniform on six atoms of mass $1/6$: for the joint law this is precisely because exactly one type accompanies each invertible residue. $\square$

**Theorem 5.5 (Full Pinning Theorem).**
$$I(p \bmod 7\,;\,T) = \log_2 3 - \tfrac23 = H(T).$$
The residue channel of the conductor-$7$ cyclic cubic field is *fully pinned*: it transmits the entire entropy of its output and attains the ceiling of Theorem 4.2.

*Proof 1 (computational).* $I = H(R) + H(T) - H(R,T) = (1+\log_2 3) + (\log_2 3 - 2/3) - (1 + \log_2 3) = \log_2 3 - 2/3$, which is $H(T)$ by Theorem 5.3.

*Proof 2 (structural).* By Corollary 3.9 the type is a function of the residue, so $w_{\mathrm{RT}}$ is supported on the graph of $T$ with row weights $v(n) = 1/6$ for $n\neq 0$ and $v(0) = 0$. Theorem 4.3 applies verbatim and yields $I = H(w_B) = H(T)$, with no logarithm evaluated anywhere. $\square$

The second proof is the conceptual one. The numerical agreement of two closed forms in Proof 1 is not a coincidence of logarithms: it is forced by determinism.

**Theorem 5.6 (Numerical certification).** $1.584 < \log_2 3 < 1.585$, hence
$$0.917 < H(T) = I(p\bmod 7; T) < 0.919 .$$

*Proof.* $2^{1584} < 3^{1000} < 2^{1585}$ as integers; take $\log_2$ and divide by $1000$. $\square$

An empirical estimate of $H(T)$ from a sample of primes returns $0.9179$ bits, and the empirical mutual information equals it to the displayed precision, as full pinning demands. Because the type is a deterministic function of the residue, the corresponding separation statistic between the two classes grows without bound with the sample size; on the reference sample it exceeds $10^4$ standard deviations, i.e. the observed "wall" between split and inert residues is not a statistical artefact but the deterministic law of Theorem 3.7 seen through a finite window.

---

## 6. The semiprime channel: exactly one label destroyed

### 6.1 Setup

Let $p, q$ be independent and uniform on the six invertible classes and $N = pq$. The observer sees $R_N = N \bmod 7$. The hidden variable is the **unordered type pair**, recorded by the number of split factors
$$S = [\,T(p)\,] + [\,T(q)\,] \in \{0,1,2\}.$$

**Definition 6.1.** $w_{\mathrm{semi}}(n, k) = \frac{1}{36}\,\#\{(u,v) \in (\mathbb{F}_7^\times)^2 : uv = n,\ S(u,v) = k\}$.

### 6.2 The group-theoretic count

The key structural remark: $T(u) = [\,u \in H\,]$ where $H = \{\pm 1\}$ is the index-$3$ subgroup of the cyclic group $\mathbb{F}_7^\times$, and the quotient $G = \mathbb{F}_7^\times/H \cong \mathbb{Z}/3$ is where multiplication lives. Write $c(u) \in G$ for the coset.

**Lemma 6.2 (Exact counts).** Let $n \in \mathbb{F}_7^\times$. Among the six ordered factorisations $n = uv$:
* if $n \in H$ (i.e. $n \equiv \pm 1$): $2$ have $S = 2$ and $4$ have $S = 0$; none has $S = 1$;
* if $n \notin H$: $4$ have $S = 1$ and $2$ have $S = 0$; none has $S = 2$.

*Proof.* $c(u)c(v) = c(n)$. If $c(n) = 1$ the possibilities are $(1,1)$ — both split, and there are $|H|^2/|H| = 2$ such factorisations — or $(\omega, \omega^2)$, $(\omega^2,\omega)$ — neither splits, $4$ factorisations. If $c(n) = \omega$ the possibilities are $(1,\omega)$ and $(\omega,1)$ — exactly one splits, $2 + 2 = 4$ factorisations — or $(\omega^2,\omega^2)$ — neither splits, $2$ factorisations. $\square$

Hence the joint table (masses out of $36$): for the two residues $n \in H$, mass $4/36 = 1/9$ at $k=0$ and $2/36 = 1/18$ at $k=2$; for the four residues $n \notin H$, mass $1/9$ at $k=1$ and $1/18$ at $k=0$.

**Lemma 6.3 (Marginals).** $\Pr[R_N = n] = 1/6$ for each invertible $n$ (multiplication by a uniform element randomises), and
$$\Pr[S=2] = \tfrac19, \quad \Pr[S=1] = \tfrac49, \quad \Pr[S=0] = \tfrac49 .$$

### 6.3 Entropies

**Theorem 6.4.** $H(R_N) = 1 + \log_2 3$; $\;H(S) = 2\log_2 3 - \tfrac{16}{9}$; $\;H(R_N, S) = 2\log_2 3 + \tfrac13$.

*Proof.* The first is uniformity on six atoms. For the second, $H(S) = \eta(1/9) + 2\eta(4/9) = \tfrac{2\log_2 3}{9} + \tfrac{8}{9}\left(2\log_2 3 - 2\right) = 2\log_2 3 - \tfrac{16}{9}$. For the third, the joint table has six cells of mass $1/9$ and six of mass $1/18$, giving
$$H = 6\cdot\tfrac{2\log_2 3}{9} + 6\cdot\tfrac{1 + 2\log_2 3}{18} = \tfrac{4\log_2 3}{3} + \tfrac{1 + 2\log_2 3}{3} = 2\log_2 3 + \tfrac13. \qquad\square$$

**Theorem 6.5 (Semiprime Degradation Theorem).**
$$I(R_N \,;\, S) = \log_2 3 - \tfrac{10}{9} = 0.4738514\ldots \text{ bits},$$
and $I(R_N;S) < H(S)$ strictly: the semiprime channel is **not** pinned.

*Proof.* $I = (1 + \log_2 3) + (2\log_2 3 - 16/9) - (2\log_2 3 + 1/3) = \log_2 3 - 10/9$. Strictness: $H(S) - I = \log_2 3 - 2/3 > 0$ since $\log_2 3 > 1.584$. $\square$

**Theorem 6.6 (Exact Deficit Theorem).**
$$H(S) - I(R_N;S) = \log_2 3 - \tfrac23 = H(T).$$
The information the residue of a semiprime fails to convey about the unordered type pair of its factors is *exactly the entropy of one factor's type*. Multiplying two primes destroys precisely one label.

*Proof.* Subtract the closed forms of Theorems 6.4 and 6.5 and compare with Theorem 5.3. $\square$

**Corollary 6.7.** $0.917 < H(S) - I(R_N;S) < 0.919$, and $0.472 < I(R_N;S) < 0.475$.

The interpretation is worth stating carefully. In the single-prime channel the observer learns the coset $c(p) \in G$ and the type is the indicator of $c(p) = 1$: perfect. In the semiprime channel the observer learns only the product $c(p)c(q)$, i.e. the image of the pair under the multiplication map $G \times G \to G$. That map has fibres of size $3$, and $\log_2 3$ bits are lost from the pair's coset information; the observable $S$, being a coarsening of the pair, recovers part of it, and the arithmetic works out to a loss of exactly $H(T) = \log_2 3 - 2/3$.

---

## 7. Which-factor blindness

Let the observer now demand the **ordered** pair $(T(p), T(q)) \in \{0,1\}^2$.

**Definition 7.1.** $w_{\mathrm{ord}}(n, \beta) = \frac{1}{36}\,\#\{(u,v) : uv = n,\ (T(u),T(v)) = \beta\}$.

**Lemma 7.2 (Exact swap symmetry).** For every $n \in \mathbb{Z}/7$ and every $\beta = (\beta_1,\beta_2)$,
$$\#\{(u,v): uv = n,\ (T(u),T(v)) = \beta\} = \#\{(u,v): uv = n,\ (T(u),T(v)) = (\beta_2,\beta_1)\}.$$

*Proof.* The involution $(u,v)\mapsto (v,u)$ preserves the product $uv = n$ (commutativity) and exchanges the two type coordinates. $\square$

**Lemma 7.3 (Ordered counts).** For $n \in H$: $4$ factorisations with $\beta = (0,0)$, $2$ with $\beta = (1,1)$, none mixed. For $n \notin H$: $2$ with each of $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$; none with $(1,1)$. (Here $1 = $ split.) Consequently the ordered-pair marginal is
$$\Pr[(1,1)] = \tfrac19, \quad \Pr[(0,0)] = \tfrac49, \quad \Pr[(1,0)] = \Pr[(0,1)] = \tfrac29 .$$

**Theorem 7.4 (Ordered entropies).**
$$H(T_p,T_q) = 2\log_2 3 - \tfrac43, \qquad H\!\left(R_N, (T_p,T_q)\right) = 2\log_2 3 + \tfrac79 .$$

*Proof.* $H(T_p,T_q) = \eta(1/9) + \eta(4/9) + 2\eta(2/9) = \tfrac{2\log_2 3}{9} + \tfrac{4(2\log_2 3 - 2)}{9} + \tfrac{2\cdot 2(2\log_2 3 - 1)}{9} = 2\log_2 3 - \tfrac43$. For the joint law, two cells carry $1/9$ and fourteen carry $1/18$, giving $2\cdot\frac{2\log_2 3}{9} + 14\cdot\frac{1+2\log_2 3}{18} = 2\log_2 3 + \frac79$. $\square$

**Theorem 7.5 (Which-Factor Blindness Theorem).**
$$I\!\left(R_N ; (T_p,T_q)\right) = \log_2 3 - \tfrac{10}{9} = I(R_N; S),$$
hence
$$I\!\left(R_N ; (T_p,T_q)\right) - I(R_N ; S) = 0 \quad\text{exactly.}$$
The residue of a semiprime reveals the *multiset* of splitting types of its two factors as well as it possibly can, and nothing whatsoever about *which* factor carries which type.

*Proof.* $I = (1 + \log_2 3) + (2\log_2 3 - 4/3) - (2\log_2 3 + 7/9) = \log_2 3 - 10/9$, equal to Theorem 6.5. $\square$

**Theorem 7.6 (The which-factor bit is real but invisible).**
$$H(T_p,T_q) - H(S) = \tfrac49 \text{ bits} > 0 .$$

*Proof.* $\left(2\log_2 3 - \tfrac43\right) - \left(2\log_2 3 - \tfrac{16}{9}\right) = \tfrac49$; note this is $\eta$-free — the $\log_2 3$ terms cancel exactly, and $4/9$ is precisely $\frac{4}{9}\cdot 1$, the entropy of a fair coin flipped on the $4/9$-probability event $S = 1$. $\square$

So the pair carries $4/9$ bits of genuine which-factor uncertainty, and the residue channel transmits exactly $0$ of them. Lemma 7.2 explains why: the channel is invariant under an involution that acts freely on precisely the which-factor coordinate and fixes everything else, so it cannot distinguish the two branches. This is a symmetry argument, and it is exact rather than asymptotic.

---

## 8. Discussion

### 8.1 Pinning as a detector of abelianness

Theorem 4.3 and its converse identify full pinning with determinism: $I(p \bmod m ; T) = H(T)$ if and only if the type map factors through $(\mathbb{Z}/m)^\times$. For a Galois extension $K/\mathbb{Q}$, the decomposition type of $p$ is determined by the Frobenius conjugacy class, and this class is a function of $p \bmod m$ for some $m$ exactly when $K$ is abelian — that is the content of the Kronecker–Weber theorem read backwards. Hence:

> Full pinning of the residue channel for **some** modulus $\iff$ $K/\mathbb{Q}$ is abelian.

For a non-abelian field — the first case being an $S_3$ cubic such as $\mathbb{Q}[x]/(x^3 - x - 1)$, of discriminant $-23$ — every residue channel has a strictly positive, computable deficit $H(T) - I(p \bmod m; T) > 0$. Information theory therefore *detects* class field theory: the deficit is an information-theoretic obstruction to abelianness, and it is computable by a finite check for each modulus.

### 8.2 Cryptographic reading

The semiprime results have a precise cryptographic content. For a semiprime modulus $N$, the residue $N \bmod 7$ (a free computation) leaks $\log_2 3 - 10/9 \approx 0.474$ bits about the pair of splitting types of the factors in the conductor-$7$ cyclic cubic field. This is not an attack — the type is a one-bit-ish invariant of each factor, not the factor itself — but it is an exactly quantified side channel, and its exactness is unusual: the leak is a closed form, not a bound.

Equally precise is the *non*-leak. Which-factor information is exactly zero for structural reasons (commutativity), not merely small. Any attempt to extract asymmetry between $p$ and $q$ from $N \bmod 7$ alone is provably futile, and would remain futile with unbounded computation.

The exact deficit theorem, $H(S) - I = H(T)$, gives a way to speak about "how much a multiplication hides" in a currency that composes: one label per multiplication, at least in this model.

### 8.3 Scope and limitations

The information-theoretic results are theorems about the *models* of Section 2.3: the uniform prime model and the uniform independent semiprime model. Their arithmetic content depends on those models being the right idealisations, which for primes is Dirichlet's theorem (asymptotic equidistribution in the six invertible classes) and for semiprimes the independence of the two factors' residues in a suitable ensemble. For a fixed finite sample the empirical values approach but do not equal the closed forms; the reference sample gives $0.9179$ against $0.918296$, and $0.4747$ against $0.473851$.

The results are also specific to conductor $7$ in their numerics — but not in their mechanism. The two-type structure comes from $[\mathbb{F}_7^\times : \{\pm1\}] = 3$ being prime; for a general prime conductor $m$, the real subfield $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m + \zeta_m^{-1})$ has degree $(m-1)/2$ and the type spectrum is richer, but the pinning theorem (Theorem 4.3 applied to a deterministic type map) survives verbatim.

---

## 9. Open problems and future work

**Conjecture 9.1 (Chebyshev factorisation of the real cyclotomic tower).** For every odd prime $m$, the Chebyshev-type coefficient $A_m(t)$ (defined by $A_0 = 0$, $A_1 = 1$, $A_{n+2} = tA_{n+1} - A_n$) factors as
$$A_m(t) = \Psi_m(t)\cdot(-1)^{(m-1)/2}\Psi_m(-t),$$
where $\Psi_m$ is the minimal polynomial of $\zeta_m + \zeta_m^{-1}$; moreover $A_{m-1}(t) + 1 = \Psi_m(t)\cdot R_m(t)$ with $R_m$ coprime to $\Psi_m$ modulo every prime $p \nmid m$. Consequently $\Psi_m$ has a root modulo $p$ iff $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod m$, uniformly in $m$.

The heuristic is that $A_m$ cuts out the "order-$m$ locus" of the trace map on $SL_2$, whose two branches correspond to $\zeta + \zeta^{-1}$ and $-(\zeta+\zeta^{-1})$; the side condition $A_{m-1} = -1$ discards the second branch. The statement is one about $\mathbb{Z}[t]$, amenable to a resultant computation, and it has been verified by direct expansion for $m = 5, 7, 11$, where the Bézout identity between the two spurious factors is integral.

**Conjecture 9.2 (Pinning–abelianness dichotomy).** Let $K/\mathbb{Q}$ be Galois and $T(p)$ the decomposition type of an unramified $p$. There exists a modulus $m$ with $I(p \bmod m ; T) = H(T)$ if and only if $K/\mathbb{Q}$ is abelian. For non-abelian $K$ — first case an $S_3$ cubic such as $x^3 - x - 1$ — every residue channel satisfies $I(p \bmod m; T) < H(T)$ strictly, with a computable positive deficit.

The forward direction is Theorem 4.3 plus Kronecker–Weber; the negative half is, for each $m$, a finite verification that the type map does not factor through $(\mathbb{Z}/m)^\times$, together with a uniform lower bound on the deficit.

**Problem 9.3 (Higher conductors and richer type spectra).** Compute the exact channel invariants for $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m + \zeta_m^{-1})$ for general prime $m$, where the type of $p$ is the order of $p$ in $\mathbb{F}_m^\times/\{\pm1\}$. One expects $H(T)$ to be the entropy of the order distribution in a cyclic group of order $(m-1)/2$, and full pinning to persist for all $m$.

**Problem 9.4 (Deficit under $k$-fold products).** Generalise Theorem 6.6: if $N = p_1\cdots p_k$ with independent uniform factors, is the deficit between the entropy of the unordered type multiset and the transmitted information again an exact multiple of a natural entropy? The $k = 2$ answer is exactly $H(T)$; the pattern for $k \ge 3$ is open.

**Problem 9.5 (Non-uniform inputs).** Replace the uniform prime model by a biased one (e.g. primes in a fixed short interval, or primes weighted by a smooth cutoff). Theorem 4.3 is distribution-free, so full pinning is unaffected; but the semiprime deficit is not, and its dependence on the input law is an explicit optimisation problem over the $6$-simplex.

---

## 10. Conclusion

For the conductor-$7$ cyclic cubic field, the passage from a prime's residue to its splitting behaviour is a perfect information channel: it delivers $\log_2 3 - 2/3 = 0.918296\ldots$ bits, which is exactly the entropy of what there is to know. The reason is structural — the law is a function, and functions saturate the data-processing ceiling — rather than a numerical coincidence between two logarithms. Feeding the channel a product of two primes degrades it by exactly one type entropy, leaving $\log_2 3 - 10/9 = 0.473851\ldots$ bits about the multiset of factor types, and by an exact symmetry it leaves precisely zero bits about which factor is which, even though $4/9$ of a bit of which-factor uncertainty is objectively present. Determinism, degradation, and blindness — all three in closed form.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Motivation}

Splitting laws in abelian number fields are usually stated qualitatively: the decomposition type of an unramified prime depends only on its residue class modulo the conductor. That is a statement about determination. It says nothing about \emph{how much} is determined, nor how the determination degrades under natural operations on the input.

We take the quantitative view, treating
\[
p\longmapsto T(p)=\text{decomposition type of }p\text{ in }K
\]
as a communication channel with input $p\bmod m$ and output $T$, and computing its Shannon invariants exactly, in bits, for the simplest cyclic cubic field $K=\QQ(\zeta_7+\zeta_7^{-1})$ of conductor $7$. Three phenomena emerge, all exact expressions in $\log_2 3$ and rationals:
\begin{itemize}
\item the channel attains its information-theoretic ceiling exactly (\emph{full pinning});
\item replacing the prime input by a product of two primes loses information equal, on the nose, to one type entropy;
\item the loss is entirely concentrated in the ``which factor is which'' coordinate, which loses \emph{all} of its information while the multiset coordinate retains the maximum possible.
\end{itemize}

\section{Notation and the entropy formalism}

\subsection{Entropy}

For $x\in\RR$ set $\eta(x)=-x\log_2 x$ for $x>0$ and $\eta(0)=0$, and for a finite index set $\Lambda$ and $w:\Lambda\to\RR_{\ge0}$ put $H(w)=\sum_{\lambda}\eta(w(\lambda))$. For a probability vector this is Shannon entropy in bits. The single analytic input is:

\begin{lemma}[Merging loses entropy]\label{lem:merge}
For nonnegative reals $w_1,\dots,w_k$ with $s=\sum_i w_i \le 1$ one has $\eta(s)\le\sum_i\eta(w_i)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Since $0\le w_i\le s$ we have $-\log_2 w_i\ge-\log_2 s$, hence $\eta(w_i)=w_i(-\log_2 w_i)\ge w_i(-\log_2 s)$. Summing over $i$ gives $\sum_i\eta(w_i)\ge s(-\log_2 s)=\eta(s)$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Joint laws and mutual information}

For finite sets $A,B$ and $w:A\times B\to\RR_{\ge0}$ write $w_A(a)=\sum_b w(a,b)$, $w_B(b)=\sum_a w(a,b)$, and
\[
I(w)=H(w_A)+H(w_B)-H(w).
\]

\subsection{Probabilistic models}

The \emph{uniform prime model}: $R=p\bmod 7$ is uniform on the six invertible classes, as furnished asymptotically by Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions. The \emph{uniform semiprime model}: $p,q$ independent and uniform on the six invertible classes, and the observer sees $R_N=pq\bmod 7$; all $36$ ordered pairs are equally likely.

\section{The arithmetic layer: two types and a deterministic law}

\begin{definition}
$f(x)=x^3+x^2-2x-1$ and $K=\QQ[x]/(f)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Cyclotomic substitution]\label{prop:subst}
For any field $L$ and nonzero $y\in L$,
\[
y^3 f\!\left(y+y^{-1}\right)=1+y+y^2+y^3+y^4+y^5+y^6 .
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Expand $(y+y^{-1})^3+(y+y^{-1})^2-2(y+y^{-1})-1$ and multiply by $y^3$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
If $y^7=1$ and $y\neq1$ then $y+y^{-1}$ is a root of $f$. In particular $\zeta_7+\zeta_7^{-1}=2\cos(2\pi/7)$ is a root; $f$ is irreducible over $\QQ$ (already modulo $2$), so $K$ is the real subfield of $\QQ(\zeta_7)$, cyclic cubic of conductor $7$.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{Splitting is all-or-nothing}

\begin{definition}[Frobenius twist]
$\tau(x)=x^2-2$, the polynomial shadow of $\zeta+\zeta^{-1}\mapsto\zeta^2+\zeta^{-2}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:twist}
Over any commutative ring, $f(x)=0$ implies $f(x^2-2)=0$. In an integral domain with $7\neq0$, moreover $x^2-2\neq x$ and $(x^2-2)^2-2\neq x$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The first claim is the polynomial identity expressing $f(x^2-2)$ as a multiple of $f(x)$. For the rest: $x^2-2=x$ together with $f(x)=0$ eliminates to $7=0$, and similarly for $\tau^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[All-or-nothing splitting]\label{thm:aon}
Let $D$ be an integral domain with $7\neq0$. If $f$ has a root $x\in D$ then $x,\tau(x),\tau^2(x)$ are three distinct roots and
\[
f(X)=(X-x)(X-\tau(x))(X-\tau^2(x)).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:twist} the three elements are roots and pairwise distinct; a monic cubic with three distinct roots in a domain factors as stated.
\end{proof}

Hence for $p\neq7$ the factorisation type of $f$ modulo $p$ is either three linear factors or irreducible: residue degrees are all $1$ or all $3$; the pattern $1+2$ never occurs.

\subsection{The splitting criterion}

\begin{theorem}[Cyclic cubic splitting criterion]\label{thm:split}
Let $p\neq7$ be prime. Then $f$ has a root in $\FF_p$ if and only if $p\equiv\pm1\pmod 7$. Equivalently, $p$ splits completely in $K$ (residue degree $1$) iff $p\equiv\pm1\pmod 7$, and is inert (residue degree $3$) otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$, $p\equiv1$.) $\FF_p^\times$ is cyclic of order divisible by $7$, so contains $y$ of order $7$; then $x=y+y^{-1}$ is a root by Proposition~\ref{prop:subst}.

($\Leftarrow$, $p\equiv-1$.) $\FF_{p^2}^\times$ has order $p^2-1$ divisible by $7$; take $y$ of order $7$ and $x=y+y^{-1}$. Frobenius sends $y\mapsto y^p=y^{-1}$, so it fixes $x$; hence $x\in\FF_p$ and $f(x)=0$.

($\Rightarrow$.) Let $f(x)=0$ with $x\in\FF_p$ and let $M=\begin{pmatrix}x&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $\det M=1$, $\tr M=x$, $M^2=xM-I$. Iterating gives $M^{n+1}=A_{n+1}(x)M-A_n(x)I$, where $A_0=0$, $A_1=1$, $A_{n+2}=tA_{n+1}-A_n$. One has $A_7(t)=t^6-5t^4+6t^2-1$ and $A_6(t)=t^5-4t^3+3t$, together with the polynomial identities
\[
A_7(t)=-f(t)f(-t),\qquad A_6(t)+1=f(t)\left(t^2-t-1\right),
\]
so $f(x)=0$ forces $A_7(x)=0$ and $A_6(x)=-1$, i.e.\ $M^7=I$ while $M\neq I$: $M$ has order exactly $7$ in $SL_2(\FF_p)$. A non-scalar element of order $m$ coprime to $p$ has eigenvalues that are primitive $m$-th roots of unity in $\FF_{p^2}^\times$, a cyclic group of order $p^2-1$; hence $m\mid p^2-1$. With $m=7$: $7\mid(p-1)(p+1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Type map]
For nonzero $r\in\ZZ/7$ let $d(r)=1$ if $r\in\{1,6\}$ and $d(r)=3$ otherwise, and let $T(r)=[\,d(r)=1\,]$.
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}[Only two types; determinism]\label{cor:det}
$d(r)\in\{1,3\}$, and $p\equiv q \pmod 7$ implies $d(p)=d(q)$: the type is a \emph{function} of the residue class.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{The conductor-free mechanism}

\begin{theorem}[Trace-order criterion]\label{thm:traceorder}
Let $p,m$ be primes, $m$ odd, $m\neq p$, and $C(t)=\begin{pmatrix}t&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item there is $t\in\FF_p$ with $A_m(t)=0$ and $A_{m-1}(t)=-1$;
\item $C(t)$ has order exactly $m$ in $SL_2(\FF_p)$ for some $t\in\FF_p$;
\item $m\mid p^2-1$, i.e.\ $p\equiv\pm1\pmod m$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1)$\Leftrightarrow$(2) from $C(t)^m=A_m(t)C(t)-A_{m-1}(t)I$ with $C(t)$ non-scalar. (2)$\Rightarrow$(3): eigenvalues lie in $\FF_{p^2}^\times$. (3)$\Rightarrow$(2): take $y\in\FF_{p^2}$ of order $m$ and $t=y+y^{-1}\in\FF_p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Specialisations]
For $p\neq5$: $x^2+x-1$ has a root mod $p$ iff $p\equiv\pm1\pmod5$ (golden-ratio / Fibonacci criterion). For $p\neq7$: $x^3+x^2-2x-1$ has a root mod $p$ iff $p\equiv\pm1\pmod7$, an independent second proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:split}. For $p\neq11$: $x^5+x^4-4x^3-3x^2+3x+1$, the minimal polynomial of $\zeta_{11}+\zeta_{11}^{-1}$, has a root mod $p$ iff $p\equiv\pm1\pmod{11}$.
\end{corollary}

In each case the bridge is a pair of explicit identities in $\ZZ[t]$: a factorisation of $A_m$ having the minimal polynomial $\Psi_m$ of $\zeta_m+\zeta_m^{-1}$ as a factor, and an identity $A_{m-1}(t)+1=\Psi_m(t)R_m(t)$ with $R_m$ coprime to $\Psi_m$ modulo every $p\nmid m$. Both were verified by expansion for $m=5,7,11$; see Conjecture~\ref{conj:cheb}.

\section{The information-theoretic layer}

\begin{theorem}[Marginalisation decreases entropy]\label{thm:marg}
Let $w:A\times B\to\RR_{\ge0}$ with total mass at most $1$. Then $H(w_A)\le H(w)$ and $H(w_B)\le H(w)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Split $H(w)=\sum_a\sum_b\eta(w(a,b))$ and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:merge} in each fibre: $\sum_b\eta(w(a,b))\ge\eta(w_A(a))$. Sum over $a$; the other case is symmetric.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Data-processing ceiling]\label{thm:ceiling}
$I(w)\le H(w_A)$ and $I(w)\le H(w_B)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$I(w)=H(w_A)+H(w_B)-H(w)\le H(w_A)$ using $H(w_B)\le H(w)$; symmetrically for the other bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Determinism saturates the ceiling]\label{thm:det}
Let $g:A\to B$ and $v:A\to\RR_{\ge0}$, and let $w(a,b)=v(a)$ if $b=g(a)$ and $0$ otherwise. Then
\[
I(w)=H(w_B)=H\!\left(b\mapsto\sum_{a:g(a)=b}v(a)\right).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$w_A=v$, since exactly one $b$ contributes per row, and $H(w)=\sum_a\eta(v(a))=H(v)$ because off-graph cells contribute $\eta(0)=0$. Hence $I(w)=H(v)+H(w_B)-H(v)=H(w_B)$.
\end{proof}

Theorems~\ref{thm:ceiling} and~\ref{thm:det} say: the mutual information of a channel is at most the entropy of its output, with equality whenever the output is a deterministic function of the input. For strictly positive input weights the converse holds as well, so \emph{fully pinned} and \emph{deterministic} coincide.

\section{The single-prime channel: full pinning}

\begin{definition}
With $A=\ZZ/7$ and $B=\{\text{split},\text{inert}\}$, let $w_{\mathrm{RT}}(n,b)=1/6$ if $n\neq0$ and $b=T(n)$, and $0$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Marginals]
$w_A(n)=1/6$ for $n\neq0$ and $0$ for $n=0$; $w_B(\text{split})=1/3$ and $w_B(\text{inert})=2/3$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Type entropy]\label{thm:HT}
$H(T)=\log_2 3-\tfrac23=0.9182958\ldots$ bits.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$H(T)=\eta(1/3)+\eta(2/3)=\tfrac13\log_2 3+\tfrac23(\log_2 3-1)=\log_2 3-\tfrac23$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Residue and joint entropy]
$H(R)=\log_2 6=1+\log_2 3$ and $H(R,T)=\log_2 6=1+\log_2 3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Both laws are uniform on six atoms of mass $1/6$; for the joint law because exactly one type accompanies each invertible residue.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Full Pinning Theorem]\label{thm:pin}
$I(p\bmod7\,;\,T)=\log_2 3-\tfrac23=H(T)$: the channel transmits the entire entropy of its output and attains the ceiling of Theorem~\ref{thm:ceiling}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Computationally:} $I=(1+\log_2 3)+(\log_2 3-2/3)-(1+\log_2 3)=\log_2 3-2/3=H(T)$.

\emph{Structurally:} by Corollary~\ref{cor:det} the type is a function of the residue, so $w_{\mathrm{RT}}$ is supported on the graph of $T$ with row weights $v(n)=1/6$ for $n\neq0$; Theorem~\ref{thm:det} gives $I=H(w_B)=H(T)$ with no logarithm evaluated.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Numerical certification]
$1.584<\log_2 3<1.585$, hence $0.917<H(T)=I(p\bmod7;T)<0.919$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$2^{1584}<3^{1000}<2^{1585}$ as integers; take $\log_2$ and divide by $1000$.
\end{proof}

An empirical estimate over a sample of primes returns $0.9179$ bits for $H(T)$, and the empirical mutual information matches it to the displayed precision, as full pinning demands. Because the type is a deterministic function of the residue, the separation statistic between the two residue classes grows without bound with sample size; on the reference sample it exceeds $10^4$ standard deviations, so the observed ``wall'' between split and inert residues is the deterministic law of Theorem~\ref{thm:split} seen through a finite window.

\section{The semiprime channel: exactly one label destroyed}

Let $p,q$ be independent and uniform on $\FF_7^\times$, $N=pq$, $R_N=N\bmod 7$, and let
\[
S=[\,T(p)\,]+[\,T(q)\,]\in\{0,1,2\}
\]
record the unordered pair of types.

\begin{definition}
$w_{\mathrm{semi}}(n,k)=\frac{1}{36}\#\{(u,v)\in(\FF_7^\times)^2: uv=n,\ S(u,v)=k\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Exact counts]\label{lem:counts}
Let $n\in\FF_7^\times$. Among the six ordered factorisations $n=uv$: if $n\in H$ then $2$ have $S=2$ and $4$ have $S=0$, none has $S=1$; if $n\notin H$ then $4$ have $S=1$ and $2$ have $S=0$, none has $S=2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$T(u)=[\,u\in H\,]$, and in $G=\FF_7^\times/H\cong\ZZ/3$ we have $c(u)c(v)=c(n)$. If $c(n)=1$: either both cosets are trivial ($2$ factorisations, $S=2$) or they are an inverse pair $\{\omega,\omega^2\}$ ($4$ factorisations, $S=0$). If $c(n)=\omega$: either one coset is trivial ($2+2=4$ factorisations, $S=1$) or both equal $\omega^2$ ($2$ factorisations, $S=0$).
\end{proof}

Thus the joint table has, for each of the two residues $n\in H$, mass $1/9$ at $k=0$ and $1/18$ at $k=2$, and for each of the four residues $n\notin H$, mass $1/9$ at $k=1$ and $1/18$ at $k=0$. The marginals are $\Pr[R_N=n]=1/6$ on invertible $n$, and $\Pr[S=2]=1/9$, $\Pr[S=1]=\Pr[S=0]=4/9$.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:semiH}
$H(R_N)=1+\log_2 3$, $H(S)=2\log_2 3-\tfrac{16}{9}$, and $H(R_N,S)=2\log_2 3+\tfrac13$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The first is uniformity on six atoms. Second, $H(S)=\eta(1/9)+2\eta(4/9)=\tfrac{2\log_2 3}{9}+\tfrac89(2\log_2 3-2)=2\log_2 3-\tfrac{16}9$. Third, the joint table has six cells of mass $1/9$ and six of mass $1/18$:
$6\cdot\frac{2\log_2 3}{9}+6\cdot\frac{1+2\log_2 3}{18}=2\log_2 3+\frac13$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Semiprime Degradation Theorem]\label{thm:degrade}
$I(R_N;S)=\log_2 3-\tfrac{10}{9}=0.4738514\ldots$ bits, and $I(R_N;S)<H(S)$ strictly: the semiprime channel is not pinned.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$I=(1+\log_2 3)+(2\log_2 3-16/9)-(2\log_2 3+1/3)=\log_2 3-10/9$. Strictness follows from $H(S)-I=\log_2 3-2/3>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact Deficit Theorem]\label{thm:deficit}
$H(S)-I(R_N;S)=\log_2 3-\tfrac23=H(T)$: the information that the residue of a semiprime fails to convey about the unordered type pair is exactly the entropy of one factor's type.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Subtract the closed forms of Theorems~\ref{thm:semiH} and~\ref{thm:degrade} and compare with Theorem~\ref{thm:HT}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$0.917<H(S)-I(R_N;S)<0.919$ and $0.472<I(R_N;S)<0.475$.
\end{corollary}

Interpretation: in the single-prime channel the observer learns the coset $c(p)\in G$ and the type is the indicator of $c(p)=1$. In the semiprime channel the observer learns only the product $c(p)c(q)$, the image under $G\times G\to G$, whose fibres have size $3$; the coarsening $S$ recovers part of the lost coset information, and the arithmetic leaves a deficit of exactly $H(T)$.

\section{Which-factor blindness}

\begin{definition}
$w_{\mathrm{ord}}(n,\beta)=\frac{1}{36}\#\{(u,v):uv=n,\ (T(u),T(v))=\beta\}$ for $\beta\in\{0,1\}^2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Exact swap symmetry]\label{lem:swap}
For all $n$ and all $\beta=(\beta_1,\beta_2)$, the count for $\beta$ equals the count for $(\beta_2,\beta_1)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The involution $(u,v)\mapsto(v,u)$ preserves $uv=n$ by commutativity and exchanges the two type coordinates.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Ordered counts]
For $n\in H$: $4$ factorisations with $\beta=(0,0)$ and $2$ with $\beta=(1,1)$. For $n\notin H$: $2$ with each of $(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)$. Hence the ordered-pair marginal is $\Pr[(1,1)]=1/9$, $\Pr[(0,0)]=4/9$, $\Pr[(1,0)]=\Pr[(0,1)]=2/9$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Ordered entropies]\label{thm:ordH}
$H(T_p,T_q)=2\log_2 3-\tfrac43$ and $H(R_N,(T_p,T_q))=2\log_2 3+\tfrac79$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$H(T_p,T_q)=\eta(1/9)+\eta(4/9)+2\eta(2/9)=2\log_2 3-\tfrac43$. The joint law has two cells of mass $1/9$ and fourteen of mass $1/18$, giving $2\cdot\frac{2\log_2 3}{9}+14\cdot\frac{1+2\log_2 3}{18}=2\log_2 3+\frac79$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Which-Factor Blindness Theorem]\label{thm:blind}
$I(R_N;(T_p,T_q))=\log_2 3-\tfrac{10}{9}=I(R_N;S)$, hence
\[
I\!\left(R_N;(T_p,T_q)\right)-I(R_N;S)=0 \quad\text{exactly.}
\]
The residue reveals the multiset of factor types as well as it possibly can, and nothing at all about which factor carries which type.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$I=(1+\log_2 3)+(2\log_2 3-4/3)-(2\log_2 3+7/9)=\log_2 3-10/9$, which is the value of Theorem~\ref{thm:degrade}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The which-factor bit is real but invisible]
$H(T_p,T_q)-H(S)=\tfrac49$ bits $>0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\left(2\log_2 3-\tfrac43\right)-\left(2\log_2 3-\tfrac{16}9\right)=\tfrac49$: the transcendental parts cancel, and $4/9$ is exactly one fair bit on the event $S=1$ of probability $4/9$.
\end{proof}

Lemma~\ref{lem:swap} explains the vanishing: the channel is invariant under an involution acting freely on precisely the which-factor coordinate and fixing everything else, so it cannot distinguish the branches. The argument is exact, not asymptotic.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{Pinning as a detector of abelianness}

Theorem~\ref{thm:det} and its converse identify full pinning with determinism: $I(p\bmod m;T)=H(T)$ if and only if the type map factors through $(\ZZ/m)^\times$. For Galois $K/\QQ$ the decomposition type is a function of the Frobenius class, and this class is a function of $p\bmod m$ for some $m$ exactly when $K$ is abelian --- the Kronecker--Weber theorem read backwards. Hence full pinning for some modulus is equivalent to abelianness, and for a non-abelian field, first case an $S_3$ cubic such as $\QQ[x]/(x^3-x-1)$ of discriminant $-23$, every residue channel has a strictly positive computable deficit. Information theory detects class field theory.

\subsection{Cryptographic reading}

For a semiprime modulus $N$, the freely computable residue $N\bmod7$ leaks exactly $\log_2 3-10/9\approx0.474$ bits about the pair of splitting types of the factors in the conductor-$7$ cyclic cubic field. This is not an attack --- the type is a coarse invariant, not the factor --- but it is an exactly quantified side channel, and the leak is a closed form rather than a bound. Equally precise is the non-leak: which-factor information is exactly zero for structural reasons (commutativity), so no amount of computation extracts asymmetry between $p$ and $q$ from $N\bmod7$ alone. The exact deficit theorem gives a composable currency for ``how much a multiplication hides'': one label per multiplication, in this model.

\subsection{Scope and limitations}

The information-theoretic statements are theorems about the two models of Section~2.3. Their arithmetic content depends on those idealisations: Dirichlet equidistribution for primes, and independence of factor residues for semiprimes. On a finite sample the empirical values approach but do not equal the closed forms ($0.9179$ against $0.918296$; $0.4747$ against $0.473851$). The numerics are specific to conductor $7$, but the mechanism is not: two types arise because $[\FF_7^\times:\{\pm1\}]=3$ is prime, while the pinning theorem, being an instance of Theorem~\ref{thm:det}, survives for every abelian field verbatim.

\section{Open problems}

\begin{conjecture}[Chebyshev factorisation of the real cyclotomic tower]\label{conj:cheb}
For every odd prime $m$, with $A_0=0$, $A_1=1$, $A_{n+2}=tA_{n+1}-A_n$ and $\Psi_m$ the minimal polynomial of $\zeta_m+\zeta_m^{-1}$,
\[
A_m(t)=\Psi_m(t)\cdot(-1)^{(m-1)/2}\Psi_m(-t),
\qquad
A_{m-1}(t)+1=\Psi_m(t)R_m(t)
\]
with $R_m$ coprime to $\Psi_m$ modulo every prime $p\nmid m$. Consequently $\Psi_m$ has a root modulo $p$ iff $p\equiv\pm1\pmod m$, uniformly in $m$.
\end{conjecture}

Heuristically $A_m$ cuts out the order-$m$ locus of the trace map on $SL_2$, whose two branches correspond to $\zeta+\zeta^{-1}$ and $-(\zeta+\zeta^{-1})$; the side condition $A_{m-1}=-1$ discards the second. The statement lives in $\ZZ[t]$ and is amenable to a resultant computation; it was verified by expansion for $m=5,7,11$, where the relevant B\'ezout identity is integral.

\begin{conjecture}[Pinning--abelianness dichotomy]
Let $K/\QQ$ be Galois with decomposition type $T(p)$ for unramified $p$. There is a modulus $m$ with $I(p\bmod m;T)=H(T)$ if and only if $K/\QQ$ is abelian; for non-abelian $K$ every residue channel satisfies $I(p\bmod m;T)<H(T)$ strictly with a computable positive deficit.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{problem}[Higher conductors]
Compute the exact channel invariants for $\QQ(\zeta_m+\zeta_m^{-1})$ with $m$ prime, where the type of $p$ is the order of $p$ in $\FF_m^\times/\{\pm1\}$.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Deficit under $k$-fold products]
For $N=p_1\cdots p_k$ with independent uniform factors, is the deficit between the entropy of the unordered type multiset and the transmitted information again an exact multiple of a natural entropy? For $k=2$ it is exactly $H(T)$.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Non-uniform inputs]
Replace the uniform prime model by a biased one. Full pinning is unaffected (Theorem~\ref{thm:det} is distribution-free), but the semiprime deficit is, and its dependence on the input law is an explicit optimisation over the $6$-simplex.
\end{problem}

\section{Conclusion}

For the conductor-$7$ cyclic cubic field, the passage from a prime's residue to its splitting behaviour is a perfect information channel: it delivers $\log_2 3-2/3=0.918296\ldots$ bits, exactly the entropy of what there is to know, and it does so because the law is a function --- functions saturate the data-processing ceiling --- not because two logarithms coincide. Feeding the channel a product of two primes degrades it by exactly one type entropy, leaving $\log_2 3-10/9=0.473851\ldots$ bits about the multiset of factor types, and by an exact symmetry it leaves precisely zero bits about which factor is which, even though $4/9$ of a bit of which-factor uncertainty is objectively present.

def primes_up_to(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes < limit, by a simple sieve of Eratosthenes."""
    sieve = [True] * limit
    sieve[0:2] = [False, False]
    for n in range(2, int(limit**0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[n]:
            for k in range(n * n, limit, n):
                sieve[k] = False
    return [n for n in range(limit) if sieve[n]]

            assert root == divides == order, f"m={m}, p={p}: {root} {divides} {order}"

def empirical_prime_channel(limit: int) -> Tuple[float, float, int]:
    """Estimate H(T) and I(p mod 7; T) from the primes below `limit`."""
    counts: Dict[Tuple[int, bool], float] = {}
    total = 0
    for p in primes_up_to(limit):
        if p == 7:
            continue
        key = (p % 7, splits(p) if p < 3000 else predicted_split(p))
        counts[key] = counts.get(key, 0.0) + 1.0
        total += 1
    joint = {k: v / total for k, v in counts.items()}
    marg_t: Dict[bool, float] = {}
    for (_, t), w in joint.items():
        marg_t[t] = marg_t.get(t, 0.0) + w
    return entropy(marg_t.values()), mutual_information(joint), total


def empirical_semiprime_channel(limit: int) -> float:
    """Estimate I(N mod 7; S) from products of pairs of primes below `limit`."""
    ps = [p for p in primes_up_to(limit) if p != 7]
    counts: Dict[Tuple[int, int], float] = {}
    total = 0
    for i, p in enumerate(ps):
        for q in ps[i:]:
            key = ((p * q) % 7, int(predicted_split(p)) + int(predicted_split(q)))
            counts[key] = counts.get(key, 0.0) + 1.0
            total += 1
    joint = {k: v / total for k, v in counts.items()}
    return mutual_information(joint)

from __future__ import annotations

from math import log2
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple


def primes_up_to(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    sieve = [True] * limit
    sieve[0:2] = [False, False]
    for n in range(2, int(limit ** 0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[n]:
            for k in range(n * n, limit, n):
                sieve[k] = False
    return [n for n in range(limit) if sieve[n]]


def eta(x: float) -> float:
    return 0.0 if x <= 0.0 else -x * log2(x)


def entropy(weights) -> float:
    return sum(eta(w) for w in weights)


def mutual_information(joint: Dict[Tuple[int, int], float]) -> float:
    mx: Dict[int, float] = {}
    my: Dict[int, float] = {}
    for (x, y), w in joint.items():
        mx[x] = mx.get(x, 0.0) + w
        my[y] = my.get(y, 0.0) + w
    return entropy(mx.values()) + entropy(my.values()) - entropy(joint.values())


def root_count(coeffs: Sequence[int], p: int) -> int:
    """Number of roots in F_p of the polynomial with ascending coefficients."""
    count = 0
    for x in range(p):
        acc = 0
        for c in reversed(coeffs):
            acc = (acc * x + c) % p
        if acc == 0:
            count += 1
    return count


def channel(coeffs: Sequence[int], bad: Sequence[int], m: int, limit: int):
    """Empirical (H(T), I(p mod m ; T), deficit) from the primes below `limit`."""
    joint: Dict[Tuple[int, int], float] = {}
    total = 0
    for p in primes_up_to(limit):
        if p in bad or p % m == 0:
            continue
        key = (p % m, root_count(coeffs, p))
        joint[key] = joint.get(key, 0.0) + 1.0
        total += 1
    joint = {k: v / total for k, v in joint.items()}
    my: Dict[int, float] = {}
    for (_, t), w in joint.items():
        my[t] = my.get(t, 0.0) + w
    h = entropy(my.values())
    info = mutual_information(joint)
    return h, info, h - info

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from math import log2

class Exact:
    """The number a + b * log2(3) with a, b rational."""

    __slots__ = ("a", "b")

    def __init__(self, a: Fraction = Fraction(0), b: Fraction = Fraction(0)) -> None:
        self.a = Fraction(a)
        self.b = Fraction(b)

    def __add__(self, other: "Exact") -> "Exact":
        return Exact(self.a + other.a, self.b + other.b)

    def __sub__(self, other: "Exact") -> "Exact":
        return Exact(self.a - other.a, self.b - other.b)

    def __rmul__(self, c: Fraction) -> "Exact":
        return Exact(Fraction(c) * self.a, Fraction(c) * self.b)

    def value(self) -> float:
        return float(self.a) + float(self.b) * log2(3.0)

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.a} + ({self.b})*log2(3)  = {self.value():.9f}"


def factor_23(m: Fraction) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Write m = 2^i * 3^j; raise if m has another prime factor."""
    num, den = m.numerator, m.denominator
    i = j = 0
    for p, sign in ((num, 1), (den, -1)):
        while p % 2 == 0:
            p //= 2
            i += sign
        while p % 3 == 0:
            p //= 3
            j += sign
        if p != 1:
            raise ValueError(f"mass {m} is not of the form 2^i 3^j")
    return i, j


def eta_exact(m: Fraction) -> Exact:
    """-m log2 m as an element of Q + Q log2 3."""
    if m == 0:
        return Exact()
    i, j = factor_23(m)
    return Exact(-m * i, -m * j)


def entropy_exact(weights: Iterable[Fraction]) -> Exact:
    total = Exact()
    for w in weights:
        total = total + eta_exact(w)
    return total


def mutual_information_exact(joint: Dict[Tuple[Hashable, Hashable], Fraction]) -> Exact:
    mx: Dict[Hashable, Fraction] = {}
    my: Dict[Hashable, Fraction] = {}
    for (x, y), w in joint.items():
        mx[x] = mx.get(x, Fraction(0)) + w
        my[y] = my.get(y, Fraction(0)) + w
    return entropy_exact(mx.values()) + entropy_exact(my.values()) - entropy_exact(joint.values())

    return u % 7 in (1, 6)

    A_0 = 0,  A_1 = 1,  A_{n+2}(t) = t A_{n+1}(t) - A_n(t)

satisfy  C(t)^{n+1} = A_{n+1}(t) C(t) - A_n(t) I  for the companion matrix
C(t) = [[t,-1],[1,0]] of Y^2 - tY + 1, which has determinant 1 and trace t.
Hence C(t) has order exactly m iff A_m(t) = 0 and A_{m-1}(t) = -1, and such an
element of SL_2(F_p) exists iff m | p^2 - 1, i.e. iff p = +-1 (mod m).

Three routines are provided, of increasing speed:
  * search_trace(m, p)     -- O(p * m) field operations, brute force over t;
  * has_order_m(m, p)      -- O(1), the closed criterion m | p^2 - 1;
  * psi_has_root(m, p)     -- O(p * deg Psi_m), independent brute force,
                              used to cross-check the two above.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

# minimal polynomials of zeta_m + zeta_m^{-1}, coefficients in ascending degree
PSI: Dict[int, Tuple[int, ...]] = {
    3: (1, 1),                        # x + 1
    5: (-1, 1, 1),                    # x^2 + x - 1
    7: (-1, -2, 1, 1),                # x^3 + x^2 - 2x - 1
    11: (1, 3, -3, -4, 1, 1),         # x^5 + x^4 - 4x^3 - 3x^2 + 3x + 1
    13: (-1, 3, 6, -4, -5, 1, 1),      # x^6 + x^5 - 5x^4 - 4x^3 + 6x^2 + 3x - 1
}


def cheb_A(t: int, n: int, p: int) -> int:
    """A_n(t) mod p, computed by the three-term recursion in O(n) steps."""
    a, b = 0 % p, 1 % p
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, (t * b - a) % p
    return a


def search_trace(m: int, p: int) -> Optional[int]:
    """Return some t in F_p with A_m(t) = 0 and A_{m-1}(t) = -1, or None."""
    for t in range(p):
        if cheb_A(t, m, p) == 0 and cheb_A(t, m - 1, p) == (p - 1) % p:
            return t
    return None


def has_order_m(m: int, p: int) -> bool:
    """The closed criterion: an order-m element of SL_2(F_p) exists iff m | p^2 - 1."""
    return (p * p - 1) % m == 0


def psi_has_root(m: int, p: int) -> bool:
    """Does Psi_m have a root modulo p?  (Horner evaluation at every point.)"""
    coeffs: Sequence[int] = PSI[m]
    for x in range(p):
        acc = 0
        for c in reversed(coeffs):
            acc = (acc * x + c) % p
        if acc == 0:
            return True
    return False


def primes_up_to(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    sieve = [True] * limit
    sieve[0:2] = [False, False]
    for n in range(2, int(limit ** 0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[n]:
            for k in range(n * n, limit, n):
                sieve[k] = False
    return [n for n in range(limit) if sieve[n]]


def cross_check(limit: int = 300) -> int:
    """Verify the three criteria agree for every available m and every odd p < limit."""
    checks = 0
    for m in PSI:
        if m == 3:
            continue
        for p in primes_up_to(limit):
            if p in (2, m):
                continue
            a = search_trace(m, p) is not None
            b = has_order_m(m, p)
            c = psi_has_root(m, p)
            assert a == b == c, (m, p, a, b, c)
            checks += 1
    return checks

from math import log2

def eta(x: float) -> float:
    return 0.0 if x <= 0.0 else -x * log2(x)


def entropy(weights) -> float:
    return sum(eta(w) for w in weights)


def marginals(joint: Dict[Tuple[Hashable, Hashable], float]):
    mx: Dict[Hashable, float] = {}
    my: Dict[Hashable, float] = {}
    for (x, y), w in joint.items():

        mx[x] = mx.get(x, 0.0) + w
        my[y] = my.get(y, 0.0) + w
    return mx, my

    mx, my = marginals(joint)

    seen: Dict[Hashable, Hashable] = {}
    for (x, y), w in joint.items():
        if w <= 0.0:
            continue
        if x in seen and seen[x] != y:
            return False
        seen[x] = y
    return True

def eta(x: float) -> float:

def root_count(coeffs: Sequence[int], p: int) -> int:
    c = 0
    for x in range(p):
        acc = 0
        for a in reversed(coeffs):
            acc = (acc * x + a) % p
        if acc == 0:
            c += 1
    return c

            types: Dict[int, int]) -> float:

    for p in primes:
        if p in bad or p % m == 0:
            continue
        key = (p % m, types[p])
        joint[key] = joint.get(key, 0.0) + 1.0

    my: Dict[int, float] = {}

## Or: what a remainder mod 7 knows, and what a multiplication forgets

Pick a prime — say $29$ — and divide it by $7$. The remainder is $1$. That single, free
computation determines, with *no* residual uncertainty, how $29$ behaves inside the number
field generated by a root of

$$f(x) = x^3 + x^2 - 2x - 1 .$$

This page is a guided tour of that fact and of its exact information-theoretic content:
how many bits the remainder carries, what happens to those bits when you multiply two
primes together, and why the answer to "which of the two factors is which?" is *exactly
zero bits* — not approximately zero, exactly.

---

## 1. The field, in one paragraph

Take the seventh roots of unity $\zeta^k = e^{2\pi i k/7}$ and form
$\alpha = \zeta + \zeta^{-1} = 2\cos(2\pi/7)$. From the identity
$y^3 f(y + y^{-1}) = 1 + y + \cdots + y^6$, valid for every $y \neq 0$, any seventh root of
unity other than $1$ produces a root of $f$. So $\alpha$ is a root of the cubic above, and
$K = \mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ is a three-dimensional field over $\mathbb{Q}$ — the *real cyclic
cubic field of conductor $7$*, the real part of the seventh cyclotomic field.

<details>
<summary>Why is <em>f</em> irreducible, and why is the field cyclic?</summary>

$f$ has no root modulo $2$ (check $f(0) = -1$, $f(1) = -1$ in $\mathbb{F}_2$), so it is
irreducible mod $2$ and hence over $\mathbb{Q}$. The three roots are
$2\cos(2\pi k/7)$ for $k = 1,2,3$, and the substitution $x \mapsto x^2 - 2$ — the shadow of
$\zeta + \zeta^{-1} \mapsto \zeta^2 + \zeta^{-2}$ — permutes them cyclically. That
three-cycle generates the Galois group, which is therefore $\mathbb{Z}/3$: the extension is
abelian, indeed cyclic.
</details>

---

## 3. Two types, and the reason there are only two

> **The Cyclic Cubic Splitting Criterion.** For a prime $p \neq 7$, the cubic
> $x^3 + x^2 - 2x - 1$ has a root modulo $p$ — equivalently, $p$ splits completely in $K$
> with residue degree $1$ — if and only if $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 7$. Otherwise $f$ is
> irreducible mod $p$ and $p$ is inert, with residue degree $3$.

Note what is *not* on the list: a factorisation into a linear times a quadratic. Splitting
is all-or-nothing, because one root manufactures three.

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the all-or-nothing argument</summary>

Suppose $f(x) = 0$ in an integral domain where $7 \neq 0$. Then $f(x^2 - 2) = 0$ as well —
a polynomial identity. Moreover $x^2 - 2 \neq x$, since combining $x^2 - x - 2 = 0$ with
$f(x) = 0$ eliminates to $7 = 0$; and likewise $(x^2-2)^2 - 2 \neq x$. So $x$, $x^2-2$, and
$(x^2-2)^2-2$ are three distinct roots, and the monic cubic splits completely.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the matrix proof of the criterion</summary>

Attach to $x$ the companion matrix $M = \begin{pmatrix} x & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ of
$Y^2 - xY + 1$: determinant $1$, trace $x$, and $M^2 = xM - I$. Iterating gives
$M^{n+1} = A_{n+1}(x)M - A_n(x)I$ with $A_0 = 0$, $A_1 = 1$, $A_{n+2} = tA_{n+1} - A_n$.
Two polynomial identities do the work:
$$A_7(t) = -f(t)f(-t), \qquad A_6(t) + 1 = f(t)\left(t^2 - t - 1\right).$$
So if $f(x) = 0$ then $A_7(x) = 0$ and $A_6(x) = -1$, i.e. $M^7 = I$ with $M \neq I$: an
element of order exactly $7$ in $SL_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$. Its eigenvalues are primitive seventh
roots of unity in $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}^\times$, a cyclic group of order $p^2 - 1$, so
$7 \mid p^2 - 1$, i.e. $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 7$. Conversely, if $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 7$,
pick $y$ of order $7$ in $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$; then $y + y^{-1}$ is Frobenius-fixed, hence
lies in $\mathbb{F}_p$, and is a root of $f$.
</details>

The argument never mentions the number $7$, which is the point of the next algorithm. See
also the general background on [splitting of primes in extensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splitting_of_prime_ideals_in_Galois_extensions)
and on [cyclotomic fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclotomic_field).

criterion at conductor $5$ ($x^2 + x - 1$ has a root mod $p$ iff $p \equiv \pm1 \bmod 5$),
our cubic at conductor $7$, and a quintic criterion at conductor $11$.

## 4. Measuring the certainty

Now model a random prime by its remainder mod $7$, uniform on the six invertible classes —
which is [Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet%27s_theorem_on_arithmetic_progressions)
in its density form. Write $R$ for the remainder and $T$ for the type.

Two of the six classes mean "split", so $T$ is a biased coin: $\Pr[\text{split}] = 1/3$.
Its [Shannon entropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entropy_(information_theory)) is

$$H(T) = -\tfrac13\log_2\tfrac13 - \tfrac23\log_2\tfrac23 = \log_2 3 - \tfrac23 = 0.918296\ldots \text{ bits}.$$

The remainder is worth $H(R) = \log_2 6$, and the *joint* entropy $H(R,T)$ is also
$\log_2 6$, because $T$ adds nothing once $R$ is known. Hence

$$I(R;T) = H(R) + H(T) - H(R,T) = \log_2 3 - \tfrac23 = H(T).$$

> **Full Pinning Theorem.** $I(p \bmod 7 \,;\, T) = H(T) = \log_2 3 - 2/3$. The channel
> transmits the entire entropy of its output.

<details>
<summary>Why this is structural, not numerical</summary>

There is a universal ceiling: for any finite joint law, merging fibres loses entropy, so
$H(\text{marginal}) \le H(\text{joint})$ and therefore $I(X;Y) \le \min\{H(X), H(Y)\}$.
And there is a universal saturation principle: if the joint law is supported on the graph of
a function $g$, with weight $v(a)$ at $(a, g(a))$, then $H(\text{joint}) = H(v) = H(X)$, so
$I(X;Y) = H(Y)$ exactly.

The splitting criterion says precisely that the type *is a function* of the residue. Full
pinning follows without evaluating any logarithm at all. The agreement of the two closed
forms is a shadow of determinism, not a coincidence.
</details>

## 5. What multiplication costs

Feed the channel a semiprime $N = pq$ with independent uniform factors, and let $S$ be the
number of split factors. The group picture makes the counting transparent: the split classes
$H = \{\pm 1\}$ form the index-$3$ subgroup of the cyclic group $(\mathbb{Z}/7)^\times$, and
knowing $N \bmod 7$ tells you the product of the two cosets in the quotient
$G \cong \mathbb{Z}/3$ — and nothing more.

| $N \bmod 7$ | factorisations with $S=2$ | with $S=1$ | with $S=0$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\in \{1,6\}$ | $2$ | $0$ | $4$ |
| otherwise | $0$ | $4$ | $2$ |

From this table: $\Pr[S=2] = 1/9$, $\Pr[S=1] = \Pr[S=0] = 4/9$, so
$H(S) = 2\log_2 3 - 16/9$, the joint entropy is $2\log_2 3 + 1/3$, and

> **Semiprime Degradation Theorem.** $I(N \bmod 7 \,;\, S) = \log_2 3 - 10/9 = 0.473851\ldots$ bits.
>
> **Exact Deficit Theorem.** $H(S) - I = \log_2 3 - 2/3 = H(T)$: multiplying two primes
> destroys *exactly one* type label — no more, no less.

> **Which-Factor Blindness Theorem.** The ordered pair $(T_p, T_q)$ has entropy
> $2\log_2 3 - 4/3$, exactly $4/9$ bits more than $S$, yet
> $I(N \bmod 7\,;\,(T_p,T_q)) = \log_2 3 - 10/9$ as well. The which-factor information is
> exactly $0$.

<details>
<summary>The one-line reason for the zero</summary>

For every residue $n$ and every type pattern $(b_1, b_2)$, the number of factorisations
$n = uv$ with $(T(u), T(v)) = (b_1,b_2)$ equals the number with $(b_2, b_1)$: the involution
$(u,v) \mapsto (v,u)$ preserves the product because multiplication is commutative. The
channel is invariant under an involution acting freely on precisely the which-factor
coordinate, so it cannot distinguish the branches. Zero, exactly.
</details>

## 7. The punchline: information theory sees class field theory

Full pinning means the type map factors through $(\mathbb{Z}/m)^\times$. For a Galois
extension, the type is a function of the [Frobenius class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_endomorphism),
and that class is a function of a residue exactly when the field is *abelian* — which is the
content of the [Kronecker–Weber theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronecker%E2%80%93Weber_theorem)
read backwards. So:

$$\text{zero deficit for some modulus} \iff K/\mathbb{Q} \text{ is abelian.}$$

non-abelian $S_3$ cubic $x^3 - x - 1$ of discriminant $-23$:

/-- `f(x) = x³ + x² − 2x − 1`, the minimal polynomial of `ζ₇ + ζ₇⁻¹`. -/
